fin_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me pull this year's closing actuals and current runway from our accounting system ({{vendor}}) so we can build next year's operating plan. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) which {{vendor}} account/organization to use, (2) the fiscal year and period range that just closed, (3) which dimensions (class, location, department, tag) I want actuals broken out by, and (4) where our current cash balance and monthly burn data lives if it's not in {{vendor}}.

Using your configured credentials, connect to {{vendor}} and: generate the full-year P&L, balance sheet, and cash-flow statement for the closing fiscal year; pull the general ledger and trial balance for that period in an open format (CSV or similar); and build a custom report grouped/filtered by the dimensions I specified (department, location, class, etc.) so we can see spend by cost center. Cross-check the P&L totals against the trial balance to confirm they reconcile. From the cash-flow statement and current cash balance, calculate current monthly burn rate and resulting runway in months.

Compile everything into a single summary document with: full-year P&L, balance sheet, cash-flow statement, dimension-level spend breakdown, GL/trial balance export reference, and a runway calculation with your assumptions stated explicitly (e.g., trailing 3-month average burn vs. last month's burn). Flag any accounts or periods where the numbers don't reconcile or look anomalous so I can review before we build the model.

Report back with: a link or file reference to the compiled summary, the headline numbers (total revenue, total expenses, net burn, cash on hand, runway in months), and a short list of any data quality issues or missing information you found. Do not proceed to drafting the next-year budget model yet — this step is limited to pulling and validating the actuals.

fin_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me draft next year's operating model and headcount plan as part of our annual budgeting process. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for (if not already provided): last year's actuals (P&L export or spreadsheet link/file), current headcount roster with salaries/loaded costs, any known growth targets or revenue assumptions for next year, and department names/leads I want line items broken out by.

2. Using the actuals, build a draft operating model (spreadsheet format) that projects next year's revenue, cost of goods/services, opex by department, and gross/operating margin, using last year's numbers as the baseline and applying any growth assumptions I gave you. Clearly label all assumptions so they're easy to challenge later.

3. Build a companion headcount plan: current headcount by department, proposed additions/departures, associated fully-loaded cost impact per hire, and cumulative headcount cost by month or quarter.

4. Flag any line items where costs grow disproportionately to revenue, or where headcount additions aren't tied to a stated business driver — these are likely negotiation points with department leads later.

5. Produce a short summary memo (half a page) highlighting total proposed budget, total headcount growth, biggest cost drivers, and open questions/assumptions that need department-lead input before finalizing.

Done looks like: a draft operating model spreadsheet, a headcount plan spreadsheet, and a summary memo, all clearly marked as DRAFT pending department-lead review and board approval. Do not finalize numbers, send anything to department leads, or submit anything to the board — this step only prepares materials. Report back with links/file locations to the three deliverables, a bullet list of key assumptions used, and any data gaps you had to estimate around.

fin_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for budget trade-off negotiations with department leads, ahead of finalizing next year's operating plan. The actual live negotiation between finance and each department lead remains a human step that you cannot perform — please only prepare the supporting materials.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: (1) last year's actuals and this year's budget model/spreadsheet location, (2) the draft headcount and spend plan by department, (3) the list of department leads and their current requested budgets/headcount, and (4) any known constraints (e.g., total spend cap, hiring freeze, growth targets).

Once you have these, produce for each department lead: a one-page briefing showing their current-year actuals vs. their proposed next-year ask vs. what finance's draft plan allocates, with the dollar and headcount gap clearly called out. Highlight the 2-3 biggest discrepancies per department and draft 2-3 possible trade-off options for each (e.g., defer a hire to Q3, swap a tool license for a cheaper one, reallocate budget from another line) with rough dollar impact for each option. Also draft a short agenda/talking-points doc for finance to use in each meeting, framing the trade-offs neutrally and noting open questions to resolve live.

Compile everything into a single document or set of documents (one section per department lead), organized so I can hand it to whoever runs each negotiation meeting. When done, report back a summary listing each department, the size of the gap, and the trade-off options you drafted, and then stop — the actual negotiation and resolution of these trade-offs remains a human step that must happen in live conversation, not something you can execute.

fin_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me circulate the annual budget deck to our board of directors via Google Slides. Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) the Google Slides link or file name of the finalized budget deck, (2) the list of board member names and email addresses, (3) the target review/reply deadline before the board meeting, and (4) any specific talking points or context I want included in the cover message (e.g. key trade-offs, headcount changes, asks for feedback).

Once you have these, do the following: open the Google Slides deck and confirm it's the correct, current version (check the title and last-edited date). Set sharing permissions so each board member has at least comment/view access, following our standard practice for board materials. Draft a concise cover email or message to the board that: states the purpose (annual budget review ahead of the board meeting), links to the deck, highlights 2-3 key decisions or trade-offs needing their attention, and states the deadline for questions or comments before the vote/consent.

Send the message and shared link to the full board list using your configured credentials, and confirm each recipient has access (no broken permissions). Log the date/time sent and the list of recipients.

Report back with: the final list of recipients, the sharing permission level granted, the exact cover message sent, confirmation the deck link works, and the deadline communicated. If any board member's email bounces or access fails, flag it explicitly so I can resolve it manually.

fin_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me track the board's review of next year's annual operating budget after I've distributed the plan. The actual board discussion and deliberation happens in their own meeting, on their own schedule — this remains a human step you cannot perform or observe directly.

What I need from you is to prepare and monitor the surrounding logistics:

1. Ask me for: the date the budget package was sent to the board, the scheduled board meeting date (if known), the primary board contact or company secretary's email, and where our board materials/communications are normally stored (e.g., Google Drive, a board portal, or shared email).
2. Draft a short, polite follow-up email I can send to the board contact confirming the meeting date/time and asking if the board has any preliminary questions on the budget before the meeting.
3. Create a simple tracking checklist (in a doc or note) listing: date sent, expected discussion date, status (pending/discussed/tabled), and space to log any questions or requested revisions that come back from the board.
4. If I give you access to a shared inbox or document store, check periodically (only when I ask you to check, or on a cadence I specify) for any incoming correspondence from the board referencing the budget, and summarize any new messages or documents you find.
5. Do not draft or send anything implying board approval, consent, or a vote — that determination is made by the board itself in their meeting and remains a human step.

When you've prepared the follow-up email draft and the tracking checklist, show them to me and stop for human sign-off before sending anything or treating the review as complete. Report back with: the draft email, the checklist, and a plain summary of what's still pending (i.e., waiting on the board's own meeting).

fin_010:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare (but NOT execute) the board consent approving next year's annual operating budget. This is a governance action that only a director can legally sign, so your job is to get everything ready for the board and then stop.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available, such as: the finalized budget model/headcount plan document, the list of current board directors and their emails, our corporate entity name, the fiscal year the budget covers, and any prior board consent template we've used (e.g., stored in Google Drive, Notion, or our cap table/governance tool). Use my configured credentials to pull these if they're accessible in connected tools.

Then do the following:
1. Draft the written consent text approving the annual budget, including entity name, fiscal year, a summary of total budget/headcount numbers, and standard resolution language ("RESOLVED, that the Board approves the annual operating budget for [FY] as presented...").
2. Prepare a one-page budget summary (top-line revenue, expense, headcount figures, and key trade-off decisions made with department leads) to accompany the consent for director review.
3. Draft a short email to the board transmitting the consent and summary for their review and signature, with a clear signing deadline.
4. Compile a checklist confirming: budget model is final, department leads have signed off, summary and consent draft are attached, and director list/emails are correct.

Do not send the consent for signature, sign on my behalf, or mark it approved — this remains a human step requiring an actual director's legal signature. Once your drafts and checklist are ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off, noting exactly what remains for me or the board to complete.
